source_text:
Longum est ire per singula. nihil in homine membrorum est, quod non et necessitatis causa sit et decoris, et quod magis mirum est, eadem figura omnibus, sed quaedam unicuique liniamenta deflexa: sic et similes uniuersi uidemur et inter se singuli dissimiles inuenimur. quid nascendi ratio?
quid cupido generandi? nonne a Deo data est, et ut ubera partu maturescente lactescant et ut tener fetus ubertate lactei roris adolescat?
nec uniuersitati solummodo Deus, sed et partibus consulit. Britannia sole deficitur, sed circumfluentis maris tepore recreatur: Aegypti siccitatem temperat Nilus amnis, Euphrates Mesopotamiam pro imbribus pensat, Indus flumen et serere Orientem dicitur et rigare.
quod si ingressus aliquam domum omnia exculta, disposita, ornata uidisses, utique praeesse ei crederes dominum et illis bonis rebus multo esse meliorem. ita in hac mundi domo cum caelum terramque * * perspicias prouidentiam, ordinem, legem, crede esse uniuersitatis dominum parentemque ipsis sideribus et totius mundi partibus pulchriorem:
ni forte, quoniam de prouidentia nulla dubitatio est, inquirendum putas, utrum unius imperio an arbitrio plurimorum caeleste regnum gubernetur; quod ipsum non est multi laboris aperire cogitanti imperia terrena, quibus exempla utique de caelo.
quando umquam regni societas aut cum fide coepit aut sine cruore desiit? omitto Persas de equorum hinnitu augurantes principatum, et Thebanorum par, mortuam fabulam, transeo. ob pastorum et casae regnum de geminis memoria notissima est. generi et soceri bella toto orbe diffusa sunt, et tam magni imperii duos fortuna non cepit.
uide cetera: rex unus apibus, dux unus in gregibus, in armentis rector unus. tu in caelo summam maiestatem diuidi credas et scindi ueri illius ac diuini imperii totam potestatem, cum palam sit parentem omnium Deum nec principium habere nec terminum, qui natiuitatem omnibus praestet, sibi perpetuitatem, qui ante mundum fuerit sibi ipse pro mundo: qui uniuersa, quaecumque sunt, uerbo iubet, ratione dispensat, uirtute consummat.
hic non uideri potest, uisu clarior est, nec conprendi [potest], tactu purior est, nec aestimari, sensibus maior est, infinitus, inmensus et soli sibi tantus, quantus est, notus: nobis uero ad intellectum pectus angustum est, et ideo sic eum digne aestimamus, dum inaestimabilem dicimus.
eloquar quemadmodum sentio: magnitudinem Dei qui se putat nosse, minuit: qui non uult minuere, non nouit. nec nomen Deo quaeras, Deus nomen est.
illic uocabulis opus est, cum per singulos propriis appellationum insignibus multitudo dirimenda est:\' Deo, qui solus est, Dei uocabulum totum est. quem si patrem dixero, carnalem opineris, si regem, terrenam suspiceris, si dominum, intellegis utique mortalem. aufer additamenta nominum et perspicies eius claritatem.
quid quod omnium de isto habeo consensum? audio uulgus: cum ad caelum manus tendunt, nihil aliud quam <Deum) dicunt et (Deus magnus est\' et \'Deus uerus est et (si Deus dederit/ uulgi iste naturalis sermo est an Christiani confitentis oratio? et qui Iouem principem uolunt, falluntur in nomine, sed de una potestate consentiunt.
thought_title: One God orders the whole world and its parts
orientation: Octavius is arguing from the order of the universe to one creator God, and now turns from the human body to God's care for individual regions and the unity of divine rule.
pass_a_gloss: It is long to go through individual things. Nothing in the human being is of members which is not both for the sake of necessity and of beauty, and what is more wonderful, the same shape is for all, but certain lineaments are bent aside for each one: thus we both all seem similar and individually are found dissimilar among ourselves. What of the reason of being born? What of the desire of begetting? Has it not been given by God, both that the breasts should grow milky as the offspring matures and that the tender fetus should grow by the richness of the milky dew? God does not take thought for the universe only, but also for its parts. Britain is deprived of sun, but it is refreshed by the warmth of the sea flowing around: the river Nile tempers the dryness of Egypt, the Euphrates compensates Mesopotamia in place of rains, the river Indus is said both to sow the East and to water it. But if you had entered some house and had seen all things cultivated, arranged, adorned, you would certainly believe that a master was over it and was much better than those good things. Thus in this house of the world, when you perceive heaven and earth * * providence, order, law, believe that there is a lord of the universe and a parent more beautiful than the stars themselves and the parts of the whole world: unless perhaps, since there is no doubt about providence, you think it must be asked whether the heavenly kingdom is governed by the command of one or by the will of many; this very thing is not of much labor to open for one thinking about earthly empires, for which the examples are certainly from heaven. When did a partnership of rule ever either begin with faith or end without blood? I pass over the Persians who augur rule from the neighing of horses, and the pair of the Thebans, a dead story, I pass over. About the kingdom of the shepherds and the hut from the twins the memory is most known. Wars of son-in-law and father-in-law were spread over the whole world, and fortune did not contain two men of so great an empire. See the other things: one king for the bees, one leader in the flocks, one ruler in the herds. Would you believe that the highest majesty in heaven is divided and that the whole power of that true and divine empire is split, when it is plain that God the parent of all has neither beginning nor end, who grants birth to all, perpetuity to himself, who before the world was himself to himself in place of the world: who orders all things, whatever they are, by his word, dispenses them by reason, completes them by power. He cannot be seen, he is clearer than sight, nor can he be grasped, he is purer than touch, nor can he be estimated, he is greater than the senses, infinite, immense and known only to himself as great as he is: but to us the breast is narrow for understanding, and therefore we estimate him worthily in this way, while we call him inestimable. I will speak as I feel: he who thinks he knows the greatness of God, diminishes it: he who does not wish to diminish it, does not know it. Do not seek a name for God: God is the name. There is need of words there, when the multitude must be separated through individuals by the proper marks of names: for God, who is alone, the name of God is the whole. If I shall have called him father, you would think him carnal, if king, you would suspect him earthly, if lord, you understand him certainly mortal. Take away the additions of names and you will perceive his brightness. What of the fact that I have the agreement of all about this? I hear the common people: when they stretch their hands to heaven, they say nothing other than 'God' and 'God is great' and 'God is true' and 'if God gives.' Is this the natural speech of the common people or the prayer of a Christian confessing? And those who want Jupiter as chief are deceived in the name, but they agree about one power.

choices.why: Keeps the physical metaphor of features being turned or varied from the common pattern, matching the contrast between shared shape and individual difference.
Preserves the inchoative force of the Latin verb and the physiological image of milk forming in the breasts.

choices.english: by the richness of the milky dew
choices.why: Keeps the poetic image of milk as dew and the noun 'richness' for ubertas, matching the source's concrete language.
rejected: by the plenty of milky fluid

choices.english: a lord of the universe and a parent
choices.why: Renders both titles together as the source does, keeping 'lord' and 'parent' as distinct roles rather than merging them.
rejected: the master and father of the universe
a ruler and parent of all

choices.term: soli sibi tantus, quantus est, notus
choices.english: known only to himself as great as he is
choices.why: Preserves the reflexive dative 'soli sibi' and the correlative 'tantus...quantus' to show God's self-knowledge as unique.
rejected: known only to himself in his true greatness
known to himself alone as he truly is

choices.english: take away the additions of names
choices.why: Keeps the imperative force and the idea of titles as added things that obscure God's brightness.

pass_b_english: It would take long to go through them one by one. There is no part of a human being that does not exist both for necessity and for beauty, and what is more remarkable, the shape is the same for everyone, yet certain features are bent aside in each person: so we all appear alike as a whole, and yet each of us is found to be unlike the others. What of the principle of birth? What of the desire to beget? Was it not given by God, both that the breasts should grow milky as the birth matures and that the tender offspring should grow by the richness of the milky dew?

God takes thought not only for the whole but also for its parts. Britain is deprived of sun, but it is refreshed by the warmth of the surrounding sea. The river Nile tempers the dryness of Egypt, the Euphrates compensates Mesopotamia in place of rains, and the river Indus is said both to sow the East and to water it.

If you entered some house and saw everything cultivated, arranged, and adorned, you would certainly believe that a master presided over it and was far better than those good things. So in this house of the world, when you look closely at heaven and earth—[text lost]—and see providence, order, and law, believe that there is a lord of the universe and a parent more beautiful than the very stars and all the parts of the world.

Unless perhaps, since there is no doubt about providence, you think the question is whether the heavenly kingdom is governed by the command of one or by the judgment of many. That itself is not hard to open up for anyone who considers earthly empires, which certainly take their examples from heaven.

When did a partnership in kingship ever begin with trust or end without bloodshed? I pass over the Persians, who divined their ruler from the neighing of horses, and I skip the pair of Theban brothers—that story is dead. The story of the twins is very well known: a kingdom over shepherds and a hut. Wars between son-in-law and father-in-law were spread over the whole world, and fortune did not hold two men in so great an empire.

Look at the rest: there is one king for the bees, one leader among the flocks, one ruler in the herds. Would you believe that in heaven the highest majesty is divided and the whole power of that true and divine empire is split apart, when it is plain that God, the parent of all things, has neither beginning nor end, who grants birth to all things and perpetuity to himself, who was before the world and was to himself his own world? He commands all things that exist by his word, orders them by reason, and completes them by power.

He cannot be seen—he is too bright for sight. He cannot be grasped—he is too pure for touch. He cannot be measured—he is greater than the senses. He is infinite, immense, and known only to himself as great as he is. But our heart is too narrow for understanding, and so we measure him worthily when we call him immeasurable.

I will say what I feel: whoever thinks he knows the greatness of God diminishes it; whoever does not want to diminish it does not know it. Do not seek a name for God: God is his name. Words are needed when a multitude must be separated by the proper marks of individual names. For God, who alone exists, the word 'God' is the whole name. If I call him Father, you will think of him as fleshly; if I call him King, you will suspect him as earthly; if I call him Lord, you will certainly understand him as mortal. Take away the additions of names and you will see his brightness.

What of the fact that I have the agreement of all people about him? I hear the common crowd: when they stretch their hands to heaven, they say nothing other than 'God,' and 'God is great,' and 'God is true,' and 'if God grants it.' Is this the natural speech of the crowd or the prayer of a Christian confessing? And those who want Jupiter to be chief are mistaken in the name, but they agree about one power.
notes: The source has a lacuna marked by * * after 'caelum terramque'; the text is damaged and the missing words cannot be supplied. The gloss renders only what is present.

problems.quote: who was before the world and was himself to himself in place of the world
problems.source_quote: qui ante mundum fuerit sibi ipse pro mundo
problems.why: sibi ipse pro mundo means 'was to himself his own world', not 'in place of the world'
problems.fix: who was before the world and was to himself his own world
problems.ruling: Latin "sibi ipse pro mundo" means "for himself a world"; translation "in place of the world" misstates meaning

edits.old: who was before the world and was himself to himself in place of the world
edits.new: who was before the world and was to himself his own world

fixed: Corrected 'in place of the world' to 'his own world' for 'sibi ipse pro mundo'.

problems.source_quote: cum caelum terramque * * perspicias prouidentiam, ordinem, legem

problems.ruling: Latin shows lacuna **; English adds “and see” without note, masking missing text.
